utterances.text: Are you aware, in your evidence, at 52:8, you said: "When I saw what the situation was, I returned to the building and I called the brigade commander Mrksic." Now you're saying you went to a vehicle.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well. Well, that's it, too. That's where I maintained communications; it was in the building itself, right next to the building, rather. That's where I had my communications. From there, I communicated.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: I won't go into that. But the reality was you spoke to Mrksic eventually?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Can I suggest, here is the following situation: One, you cannot remember hearing anything about a hospital evacuation at a briefing on the 19th at 1800 hours. Two, on the morning of the 20th, five buses arrive, individuals, clearly pre-selected, with armed guards coming from the hospital on their way to Sremska Mitrovica. Three, you have individuals who are armed threatening retribution, my word, which requires you to do something about it. So, did you ask Mrksic, who was responsible for the evacuation; namely, these people, because they're not doing their job terribly well. We've got TOs all around them threatening to basically cut their throat. Did you feel, perhaps, that might be something that your commander should be made aware of?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's why I called him, to see what to do and for how long in order to secure these buses. How come the buses are there and ...

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: No. It's not just a case about what to do. Command can be good command, can be indifferent. It can be bad, and there can be misunderstandings. People mixing up their tasks. So it didn't necessarily follow that this was only bad command; it could have been a misunderstanding of the responsibilities. So I would suggest to you, the first thing you would want to tell him is: There are no officers around here, Commander Mrksic. Did you tell him that?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what I said to the commander; that buses with people were brought to the barracks and that civilians are threatening them and that the safety and security of these people are in danger. The commander ordered me clearly to ensure the full safety and security of these people at all costs. That now there was a government meeting underway of Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem [as interpreted], and that was clear to me that I was supposed to do nothing but just to provide security. I returned to the actual spot, Predojevic stepped up the security, at that moment Maric came to the barracks with one squad, because he was supposed to return some equipment to the barracks; and together, with this warning with increased security, we got these people out of the barracks and first we repelled them from the buses and then we threw them out of barracks. So the buses were no longer in any kind of danger.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, that's all well and good. But you have five buses of pre-selected men coming from the hospital, and a bus driver in charge. Now, can we deal with reality, with the utmost respect to you. One of the questions you're either going to be asking or seeking guidance on is: Who is the officer in charge of these buses? Who do I deal with? How do I coordinate with him? That will probably be the first question out of your lips. So who was in charge? I suggest you did ask Mrksic, and I would like an answer.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Had an officer been there, I would have asked the officer there, but there was no officer there. I didn't see any. There was only the buses, the people around them, and Predojevic. Now, that's the issue, and that is what we are resolving and indeed we did resolve it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: You don't need to have an officer immediately in situ for that officer to be in charge of the buses; that is correct, isn't it? The officer can be nearby or on his way or waiting. That is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. But if we are waiting for him, then it can be too late to take any kind of security measures later.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: No. You can take your security measures and still wait. They do not necessarily go hand in glove, do they?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. And we did take these measures and secure the buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Do you have a difficulty telling this Court who you know was in charge of that convoy?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no difficulty, no difficulties. If I knew, I'd say so. But Vukasinovic did come; he was with the convoy. He came; he drove the people there. Now whether he was the one in charge of that, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, where do you hail from? Where do you come from? What country?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was born under Mount Durmitor in Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Did you know Mr. Sljivancanin, or how long did you know Mr. Sljivancanin in 1991?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew him. I met him when I came to the Guards Brigade in 1982.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Vukasinovic, if he was in charge of the transport, was the security organ at that time and subordinated to Mr. Sljivancanin. That is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the security organ. He was in the security department. Now, whether he was subordinated to him then, well, he must have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: So, is the -- the answer is that Mr. Vukasinovic, you knew, was subordinated to Sljivancanin on the 20th of November, and indeed sometime before; that is correct, you knew that?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I didn't. I knew that he was in that department but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: That department, presumably, is the security organ, is it?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: And the commander of the security organ for OG South was Mr. Sljivancanin, you knew that.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's not commander; he is the chief of security.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: And, therefore, Vukasinovic would have been under him; that is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I don't know whether -- well, when the commander was in Negoslavci, whether something was lost there; but, otherwise, he would have to be subordinated to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: You say that you contacted Mrksic; and basically although he denies that, Sljivancanin, were you not aware, that he was responsible - let's even take his account - that he was responsible for the triage down at the hospital on the morning of the 20th?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: What, you never knew that Sljivancanin was responsible for the triage, the selection procedure at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later on, they told me that he was at the hospital. Now, whether he carried it out or not, I don't know. I am not aware of what they were doing at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Well, you had radio contact, that, we know.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Did it occur to you to try and contact anyone, for example, at the hospital? For example, Paunovic?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. Paunovic was the commander responsible for securing the hospital. You knew that, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I knew that; that his unit was securing the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, if there is going to be a person who will know who's responsible, it will be Paunovic, and he's at the hospital. That is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: It's not probably; I suggest it's a certainty; isn't that right, Mr. Susic?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I don't know. I don't know. I wasn't there. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Well, then, why didn't you contact Paunovic, the man who could answer your questions for you?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not establish contact with him, because I didn't know that he was responsible for that. So why would I contact him?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Forgive me, I thought you had said in evidence earlier on that you were aware that Paunovic's battalion was responsible for the security at the hospital. Did you not say that in your evidence?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. And I'm saying it now. I'm saying that that's the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Well, if that's the way it was, he is the man who can answer your question, isn't he?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at that moment, I didn't call him. Now, whether I should have called him or not, I don't know. But I didn't call him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: What way does the presence of five buses arriving - and I will use the layman's term - arriving within your zone of responsibility, how would that affect and how does that affect the way you deal with matters?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It does affect it, because they are entering the zone of responsibility where security is provided by another company. That's where the problem occurs that has to be resolved, and we resolve it. But the only question is, for how long it is going to go on; whether we need reinforcements, whether we should ask for reinforcements or whether something else should be done there. That is why it is necessary to speak to the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Never mind about the conversation with the commander. There is a much bigger problem for you here, isn't there? You have been lumbered, to use the English word, with 250 individuals who have been preselected, men, with a hostile group baying for their blood; and they eventually will be moving on. That is right, isn't it, as far as you are aware?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the situation. Within the compound of the barracks are the buses, people are sitting on the buses, around them are civilians who are verbally abusing them and insulting them. And in order to prevent anything more serious from happening, urgent measures have to be taken to ensure the full safety and security of those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: It is right to say that there was always the possibility of a criminal act occurring against any one of them. That is also right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is right. That could have happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Consequently, if those people are to leave your zone of responsibility, you have a duty, do you not, to ensure that they are moved on safely and not irresponsibly; that is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: As it is the case that these five buses were within your zone of responsibility, did you ensure that when they were moved on, that they were going to a safe place or they would be safe, to avoid such possible criminal acts?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why would I be doing that? The basic thing for me was that they should be safe within the zone of responsibility. As for their transport, somebody else would take care of that further on. If I had received that by way of an assignment I would have resolved that assignment, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: No. No, because your evidence has been in general term terms as follows: I was contacted by a young officer, or a junior officer, Predojevic. I witnessed what was happening. I realised the responsibility of criminal acts. As a consequence, I phoned Mrksic. Mrksic said give them all security, and their future will be determined by the government. He does not and did not say anything to you about where they would go or who would control them when they left, did he?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, I would like to know what steps you took to ensure that these people, when they were moved on, were going to be safe.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I did was that as for all civilians and this group of locals, I simply removed them all from the barracks compound. It wasn't me, in actual effect; it was Predojevic with the members of his company.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: It is right you did not speak to Panic; that is correct, is it not?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Panic, Lieutenant-Colonel Panic and Major Lukic, I saw them later near the buses, not right by the buses but near the buses. Everything was peaceful then, and we were talking a bit about the fact that there had been some problems before that and that that had been redressed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Is the answer then you did speak to Panic?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But -- well, I did talk to him, but Panic knew that, too. Whatever I knew, he knew too.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Well, I would like to know what you said to Panic.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Let's see if you can remember what Panic said to you.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can't remember that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Vukasinovic? Third time lucky, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see Vukasinovic at all, but he was there, or at least they told me that he was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Well, when you spoke to Panic, that you can remember speaking, but not what you spoke about, was there any conversation about who was in charge of the convoy on its onward route?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps, but I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Well, just a moment. You have at least 250 people there and we know now, even though there will be arguments about the numbers, we know there was the most appalling slaughter some hours after they left your charge. So surely that is something that you must have thought about, but who on earth took control of these people and led them to their death in the most dreadful way? Haven't you thought about that?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at the time. Nothing was further from my mind than to even think that anything like that might happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: One of the things that definitely must have been on your mind is: Who on earth is that colonel going out the door with 250 people who have been preselected? How did you know, for example, who he was and where they were going and whether they were going to be safe?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When they came, if they had arrived in vehicles and were being loaded on to other vehicles, well, I would have thought differently. If they had been ordered to walk, I would have thought differently. But it was the same buses; the same security taking them there. It struck me as perfectly normal. When they came, I didn't even ask myself if it was the same person organising all the that. It didn't mean anything to me. It's not like they changed buses or anything or the security arrangements. Everything was the same, and they just proceeded like that which struck me as perfectly normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Well, you say that they didn't exchange or change buses. Can I suggest that we have heard evidence, and I'm going to read it for you, to see if it refreshes your memory -- forgive me one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, while my learned friend is looking for the relevant portion, may I address you please? I didn't want to interrupt, but page 48, line 9, there is a correction that needs making. The witness was talking about what Mr. Mrksic and the transcript reads that this was a meeting of the government of Slavonia, Baranja, and western Srem; whereas, the witness only said the SAO Krajina. There was no reference to the other constituent parts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: I found one part; funnily enough, not the part I wanted, but it doesn't matter. This was in relation to changing buses, because what I'm suggesting occurred was that individuals were taken from bus A to bus B, all right? And the following evidence was given at line 3649:10. "The situation had already quieted down, but this high-ranking officer, who called out our names, told us to go to the other bus that was parked about 30 metres away from the remaining buses. The paramilitaries then formed a gauntlet; and as we passed through it, they kicked us with their boots, with clubs, with iron rods, whichever way they could. We ran over to the other bus because we knew that if any of us fell to the ground, they would probably beat us to death." Well, now, you didn't see anything like that, did you, by any chance?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. But this is about Major Vukasinovic, when he sent some of the people back to the hospital, at least that's what Predojevic claims.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Well, are you saying that this account, this description agrees or accords with what you have been told by others or what you've seen yourself?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see that. I wasn't there when Vukasinovic was in the barracks, but Predojevic told me that Vukasinovic had indeed been there and that he had sent a group from those buses back. So I do know that Vukasinovic was there, at least based on other people's statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: But working on other people's statements, I have read out to you - I can do another one if you really want - read out to the facts that people were beaten, kicked, hit with rifle butts, punched, when the person you say, Vukasinovic, you say it might be another, and in actual fact there was a transfer from bus A to B. Now I'm asking you absolutely straight: Are you saying that you didn't hear about beatings when the individuals were being transferred? I'm saying you saw it, but you were told; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't told that. All I was told was Vukasinovic had been there, and he had sent a group of about 20 people back. Once we had set up a security system and we'd send those people away and chase them out, no one turned up and the situation around the buses was quite calm.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: But clearly beatings were occurring before you set up your cordon; that is correct, isn't it? Otherwise, this doesn't make sense.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't there; therefore, I don't know about that. But that's why I was taking measures; I wasn't waiting for Lukic who was elsewhere outside. I ran to the scene for this to be dealt with, and that's why Predojevic had called me to begin with saying that the situation was difficult and needed sorting out.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: So Lukic was outside; so Lukic wasn't there; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know if he was or not. But nothing was done or perhaps something was done. Be that as it may, Predojevic calls me, tells me the situation is complex. I come there; I realise that this is true and that it might come to some beating or something, which is certainly nothing that we would ever allow.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, did you ever receive a contact from Mrksic to inquire if the situation had improved? What I will call demonstrating concern of a commander? I take it that's no in the translation.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He didn't call me and I didn't report because the situation wasn't entire quiet by this time. And I realised that Lieutenant-Colonel Panic was there, Chief of Staff, and Major Lukic, and I did no more reporting.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever receive a call from Mrksic to say that he had authorised the removal of the individuals from the JNA barracks?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever receive any phone call from Mrksic saying, really to assist his subordinate commanders, exactly what had happened, that there had been a political decision and these 250 people were being taken elsewhere? Did you ever receive any call about that?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. But when we talked, he said there was a government meeting in progress and the issue was being dealt with.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: So the situation, if we just look at Mrksic's situation, is he was informed by you about behaviour of TOs, armed individuals at the JNA barracks, he says: Put security on it. And he does absolutely nothing else to ensure that any -- if everything is fine; that is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If any problems whatsoever had occurred later on, if we hadn't been able to send those people away from the buses and get them out of the barracks, if we'd had to use other methods such as physical force, then we would have told the commander. But everything went smoothly; we secured the spot. The situation was now back to normal, therefore, no need to inform anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: So according to you, so everything went smoothly and over 250 people went to their death; is that what we're talking about? Is that your idea of smoothly?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's not at all what I'm saying. That's not what I'm saying. But the situation was now calm. The same buses, the same security, the vehicle driving ahead of them, and a military APC following in their stead, and they were moving on. I had no idea what would happen next.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: And the answer --

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no way for me to even assume.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: And the answer to the original question is: Mrksic made no follow-up phone calls to let you know what was happening or expressing any concerns. That is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't call him. No one from the barracks called him about any further problems. Therefore, there was no need for that. The reason being simply the situation was now entirely peaceful.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Did you know that this bus or these buses were going to Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever inquire: Where are these buses going to, because I will have to file a report or report to my commander and/or others?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't. Why? Because this is not some sort of a bus stop so that I would have no know where those people were off to. It was just a brief respite, a rest that they were getting there, and they simply moved on the same buses that had brought them there. They were now leaving my area of responsibility and entering someone else's, and they would now be taking charge.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: But on the 20th at 1800 hours, you were going to have to go to a command meeting, weren't you, where your commander, Mr. Mrksic, was going to be hearing various reports about what was happening that day, apart from other things, obviously. That is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. I believe that Lukic reported about that, too, simply because this occurred inside the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: No, no. First question: Were you attending -- intending to attend the command briefing at 1800 hours that evening on the 20th of November?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And is it right that one of the functions of a command briefing is to gain information from your commander and also inform him with regard to your zone of responsibility, what is occurring in it, such problems, basically have an information available for him and inform him of any problems you had. That is right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: And so when it came to the command briefing, and Colonel Mrksic not having contacted you, you had a situation where you were going to go to a briefing, as you say on your evidence, that you would be saying to Colonel Mrksic and the assembled masses, other officers there, that five buses arrived; they came from the hospital, but you didn't know who was in charge of them; that you contacted -- that there were troubles with the buses; that there were irregulars threatening the buses, and you secured the situation. You would be saying that, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what the commander submitted a report on, I mean Lukic. To what extent exactly, I don't know or how extensively, simply because this occurred inside the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: No, no. You had become involved, because Lukic wasn't there. You had been in direct contact with your commander. So I would suggest if the commander asked you about what was happening, it would be: I was there. I was contacted that five buses had arrived. There was no officer there. They were misbehaving very badly; so much so, I contacted the commander. He told me to protect them, and everything calmed down. That's what you would be saying, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. Correct, I would be saying just that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: But you have a fairly major problem, don't you? Because the corollary, the next part of your account would be as follows: Actually, commander, 250 of them were taken from my zone of responsibility, and I don't know who took them. I didn't even recognise him. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't my responsibility to recognise those people. My responsibility was for the 2nd Company to secure those people for as long as they were inside the barracks. As for anything else that happened, I mean Colonel Panic Chief of Staff filed the report as is did Major Lukic, and I'm sure Vukasinovic once they were done with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Never mind Panic, never mind Vukasinovic, never mind anybody else. I'm saying to you if Mrksic was asking you: Who took those people away? You would not be able to say who it was. You would not be able to say which unit he belonged to. You would not be able to say where they were going. That is right, isn't it? And correct on all three points?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: I would suggest to you, you know perfectly well and a large number of people within the Guards Brigade know perfectly well who took those people to Ovcara, and you are all covering it up?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I, for one, am not covering anything up. I don't know who it was, nor am I interested in knowing as far as my responsibility was concerned. They were there and they moved on. My responsibility for them was as far as long as they were inside the barracks, to keep them from coming to any harm.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: And you saw the colonel who was leaving, so you say, is that correct, but you did not recognise him?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't. But he was a colonel; he had authority. He couldn't have just taken those buses away, and the security had he not had appropriate orders to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: You saw his face, isn't that correct? You saw him walking around the buses, and you saw him going out. That is correct, isn't it? That is why you say you could not recognise him.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no, the distance was considerable. I didn't recognise him. But I don't think I would have recognised him anyway, since he wasn't from the Guards unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: And the one person it was not; it was not Pavkovic, was it?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. Certainly not. I do know Pavkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Can I ask you about a piece of evidence -- or actually, before I do, can I just deal with that last piece of evidence. You said he had authority. He couldn't have just taken those buses away, and the security had he not had appropriate orders to do so. Would you accept from me that the removal of those persons had to be under the direction of Mrksic or a person subordinated to him or to whom he delegated powers? It's a long question; I'll break it up, if you want.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he must have taken those orders from someone. I don't know from whom. It certainly wasn't from me. I was in charge of nothing there, apart from securing them for as long as they were inside the barracks. Who gave him that assignment? He came in two alter rain vehicles: He did everything properly. There was one vehicle driving ahead of the buses and there was one following the buses, and they moved on. I see no error in that. It's the same vehicles, the same drivers, the same security arrangement, and they simply moved on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: And, therefore, as we were within the zone of responsibility of OG South, it had to be under the direction of Mrksic, one of his subordinates, or perhaps more accurately, one to whom he delegated powers. That is correct, isn't it? Could I have an answer, please?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I don't know. I don't know on whose orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It seems Mr. Vasic has an objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My objection was about the fact that the witness had already said he didn't know. He has just repeated that yet again for our benefit, but my objection is now of no consequence, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I would like to break that up and ask the question again. I would submit it's a perfectly valid question. There is a logical basis for it, and I would suggest and submit that this witness is obviously avoiding the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I have not sought to interfere at all, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: My apologies, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: In this trial, I at least try to keep words to the minimum.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: As indeed we all do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Susic, we were within the zone of responsibility of OG South; that is correct, isn't it? What is the answer, please?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: That these buses were coming and controlled by OG South; it's within OG South's zone of responsibility. That is correct; isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: But if actual fact you had spoken to Mrksic about it, and clearly he accepted that they were his responsibility. That is also correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: And I would suggest logically and sensibly for those people to be removed, they had to be removed under the direction of the commander of OG South, Mrksic, or to a person to whom he had delegated the powers; that is correct also, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Was that how it should have been or not, I don't know. But this colonel came and that's what they did. On whose orders, the first man's orders, the second man's orders, the third man's orders, or whoever. I don't know. But he must have taken those orders from someone, just like I had my own orders to secure them for as long as they were in the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: And that answer and the honesty of that answer, is that the same honesty that we are to apply in the rest of your evidence?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you the following question: The question was put to you, it was -- I think it was Mr. Vasic this morning: "Could he," that's Vukasinovic, "Could Vukasinovic possibly have got on to one of those buses there, without previously requesting approval from Captain Predojevic who was guarding those buses?" Do you remember that question being asked? So could Vukasinovic possibly have got on to one of those buses there, without previously requesting approval from Captain Predojevic who was guarding them? Do you remember that question?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that, because all that happened when I wasn't there. I don't know. But they told me that Vukasinovic had set to one side about 20 people and had them sent back to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: No, there's a misunderstanding. That was a question that you were asked this morning. Let me read out your answer. There seems to be a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'm sorry for interrupting but I think my question was: Did Major Vukasinovic have to report to Captain Predojevic before he got on to the bus. I think that was the phrasing of my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well I've got the transcript; I'm just reading it. It's at 12:18:

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: So this is the question you were asked. I'm reading back what you were said: "Could he," that's Vukasinovic, "possibly got on to one of those buses, without previously requesting approval from Captain Predojevic who was guarding those buses?" "A. He could have, but he was an authorised officer from a superior command. But no one else could possibly have got on to those buses. So the answer that you gave is: "He could have; he was an authorised officer from a superior command." Now that's the answer that you gave. The question that I have is this: What do you mean by Vukasinovic, he was an authorised officer from a superior command and therefore could?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because Vukasinovic was from the brigade command, and that's why he could if, on top of that, he was going with that convoy.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: So when you make that reply, is that what I would call standard military procedure; that where a superior command comes on to the zone of responsibility of a lesser command, the superior command has priority?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends -- it's not superior in every respect, but with regard to certain issues; say, if it's security, then it should -- well, it cannot be an issue of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'll ask the question. He was an authorised officer from a superior command, therefore he could. What I'm trying to devine is does that mean, therefore, is if a person comes from an authorised, from a superior command, he has superiority? Relatively simple question.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what this is about. What priority? We are not doubting him. If he got in, if he's supposed to do something, there is no reason for me to have any doubts as far as Vukasinovic or Predojevic are concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: I'm not trying to catch you out. I'm -- you smile, but I'm not. I'm merely trying to find out what you mean by this phrase. I will read the question again. It was whether Vukasinsevic could go on to the bus. Question by Mr. Vasic: "Could he," that's Vukasinovic, "possibly have got on to one of those buses there, without previously requesting approval from Captain Predojevic who was guarding those buses?" "A. He could have. He was an authorised officer from a superior command, but no one else could possibly have got on to those buses."

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Now that's the question; that's the answer. I'm merely trying to clarify that when a person is from a superior command, he can have priority by way of action and --

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Although, if the officer is from the superior command and if he came with a convoy, because I was not there when the convoy arrived. If he came with a convoy, that means that he was in charge of the convoy, so then he had the right to enter the buses, to single people out, and get out. And if he did not, then he did not. Vukasinovic, if he had come from somewhere else, he could not just board the buses, nor would he ever have doing anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Now here is a situation. Let's say it's Vukasinovic with the buses, I'm not saying he did. Let's say it's Vukasinovic with the buses, and he arrives at the barracks and there is Predojevic. Who has the priority, the superior command or Predojevic?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not the superior command. Vukasinovic is senior because he came with the convoy, and he is in charge of that convoy. He can move them from one bus to the other. Predojevic cannot; Predojevic can just secure them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Having issued him, then why do you refer to the phrase, "from a superior command" as having the priority?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Vukasinovic was from the superior command. I cannot say that he was from a subordinate command when he was from the superior command. He is from the command of the Guards Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Or OG South?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It can be put that way, too. OG South, command of the Guards Brigade; it's the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I have no further questions. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: This would be a convenient time, if you were thinking it would be useful to have a break, Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will take the second break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon to all in the courtroom. Good afternoon, Mr. Susic. I'm going to put a few questions to you in relation to some things that were unclear in my mind. Could you tell me, Mr. Susic, who was the person in charge of the barracks in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The person in charge of the barracks in Vukovar was Major Lukic, commander of the 2nd Assault Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: This responsibility of his, can you explain all the things that it entails, what are all the things that he was responsible for?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the briefest possible terms, he is responsible for the overall situation in the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Does that include -- I mean this responsibility of his, does it include security in the barracks, how people who live and work in the -- or rather of the people who live and work in the barracks, if I can put it that way, as opposed to those people who happen to find them selves there for any reason?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You were saying that there was the security of the barracks and that this was a large area where there was devastation and that is how the civilians managed to come in and you spoke about the number of civilians who were there. At these checkpoints or, rather, at these entrance desks, are records kept of people who go in and out of the barracks?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, records of kept.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: And who was responsible for the records?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is the desk that is responsible for the records or, rather, the commander of the security within the barracks there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Does the commander of the barracks have a responsibility for that too?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander of the barracks has responsibility for everything that is done within barracks, that included. However, it is the reception desk organs that do this, members of the military police who are on duty at the reception desk.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Susic, can an officer, regardless of where he comes from, and if he is from the superior command too, can he issue any orders to the commander of the barracks?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He cannot.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you saw four or five buses and that you saw civilians, some of them were armed, you describe the way in which they were clothed. The learned Prosecutor put to you some parts of statements made by certain witnesses. I'm interested in the following: While you were by this bus, and as you were taking these security measures, did you see any one of these civilians having physical contact with any one of the persons who were on the bus?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I claim with full responsibility that no one had physical contact with the persons on the bus from the moment when they were -- when security was ensured.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: A statement was put to you to the effect that members of the Yugoslav People's Army also took part in this physical showdown with the persons from the buses; did you see any such thing?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see that, and it is certainly untrue that members of the JNA in any way jeopardised these people who were on the buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You did not see when Major Vukasinovic came, you did not see him taking these people out of this bus and returning them, that was what was said. I'm interested in the following: Captain Predojevic and Major Vukasinovic, did they know each other?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did know each other, because they are both from the same unit, from the Guards Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: All right. You said something about the anti-terrorist company. When you spoke to the Prosecutor, you referred to that as well. I asked you about that, Mr. Vasic asked you about that. I'm interested in the following: This task on the 18th of November was issued -- well, you described how it was issued. As for the commander of the anti-terrorist company, did you issue any task to him for the 19th or the 20th of November?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that I did not issue any task on the 19th or the 20th to that commander with regard to any kind of security.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember whether their company commander Maric informed you about somebody else having issued him any task for the 19th or the 20th?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that, too. No one issued a task to him apart from --

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You and the brigade commander, the Guards Motorised Brigade commander, can anyone else issue any kind of order to the anti-terrorist company?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Bulatovic please turn off his microphone while the witness is speaking. Interpreter's note.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one can.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honour, we have a bit of a problem in the transcript. So in order to avoid any kind of misunderstanding, I'm going to put a question to you, Mr. Susic, once again. Listen to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Maric, as commander of the anti-terrorist company, did he inform you of anyone having issued any task to him for the 19th or 20th of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that he did not inform me about that, and no one, apart from myself, issued any tasks to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Lest there be any misunderstanding, what does that mean "apart from you?" Did you give him any task for the 19th or 20th? You have already answered that, but let's clarify.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In relation to any kind of security, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You were mentioning several times here that in your area of responsibility, you wish to secure these buses. I'm interested in what was your area of responsibility on that day, on the 20th?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The area of responsibility is where the unit disposition is. This was the company barracks. This what we are talking about, and that is secured by another company.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that every unit that has its formation in a certain disposition has its own area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Every unit has a certain area of responsibility, and it is responsible there for the security of everything that happens within that zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that the commander -- does that mean that the person who is commander of that unit, in whose area of responsibility this is, is responsible for the state of affairs in that area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we have a problem with the transcript, page 73, line 11. I think that the answer is not recorded properly, the witness's answer, so I'm going to put the question yet again.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Who secured the barracks on the 20th of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 20th of November, 1991, the 2nd APC Company secured the barracks of the 1st Battalion of the Military Police, which became part of the 2nd Assault Detachment, and the commander of that company is Captain Mladen Predojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You attended the briefing on the 20th of November, and you said that you do not recall any mention of the evacuation of the hospital. You were given some assignments. At the briefing, did you pay attention only to the tasks that you were being given? Do you note them down, or do you note down also the tasks that are given to other commanders?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At briefings, I only write down tasks that pertain to my unit, or rather, the tasks that I'm supposed to carry out with my unit. I could not note down the others, and it is not my duty to write down all the others so I did not write them down.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Susic, could you, on the basis of the behaviour of the locals at the barracks and these verbal attacks by them against the men in the buses, could you conclude whether the people on the buses had participated in combat operations in any way, and on whose side?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, one could conclude that some of them were members of paramilitary units, because people said that they were, that they had killed some of their relatives, that they had torched some of their houses, that they had been involved in certain attacks. So on that basis, one could draw such a conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: If we have a zone of responsibility and we have a commanding officer of a unit in whose zone of responsibility -- in that zone of responsibility, can it happen that a lesser commanding officer or any officer issue an order to a higher-ranking officer? Is that at all possible?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it is not possible. And it has never happened and never happened that a lesser-ranking officer issue any orders to a higher-ranking officer. Irrespective from which command they are, the commander is in charge of everything in his zone of responsibility and that was the case with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bulatovic. Mr. Susic, you will be pleased to know that that concludes the questions that are to be asked of you which means now that you are free to go and return to your other affairs. The Chamber would like to thank you for your attendance here and the assistance you've been able to give us. The court officer will show you out. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. Would you please read aloud the affirmation on the card that's given to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours, and everyone. Would you, sir, give us your name?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: I'm Ljubisa Vukasinovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether you have adjusted your headphones properly. Please feel free to do so, so that you have good audibility and not have any problems on that score. Mr. Vukasinovic, I said during our preparations that you should pause after my questions in order to avoid any overlaps and, hence, creating problems for the interpreters. I sure hope you will bear this in mind through your testimony. I shall now go through your CV. Would you please be so kind as to just confirm the truthfulness on which the date you have given me? And I apologise to the interpreters for not having provided a copy to them, and I shall try to be slow in going through your CV. You were born in 1954 in Kosovo, the municipality of Lipljani?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: That is correct, and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You completed high school as a civilian; and then in 1977, you completed the military academy?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In -- from 1994 to 1996 in pursuing your further education, you also completed the command staff school, advanced school; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And from 2000 to 2001, you completed the highest military school in the army of Yugoslavia, which is the School of National Defence; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In 1977, you were a lieutenant?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: 2nd lieutenant; and the next year, you were conferred the further rank of lieutenant?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Then until 1990, you were captain first class?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In 1990, you were conferred the rank of major, and it was with that rank that you were there when the Vukovar events unfolded?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In 1993, you were given the rank of lieutenant-colonel?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And in 1997, the rank of colonel, which you still hold today, and you are still active in the military; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a few more particulars about you. You were in service from 1977, when you completed the military academy, up to 1991. You practically held all duties in military police units from platoon commander to company commander through deputy and commander of military police battalion; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Then in the summer of 1991, you were transferred to security organs. As far as I can recall, it was sometime in August that you were transferred to the Guards Brigade security organ; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Until the end of 1992, you were assistant head of security for staff security affairs in the Guards Brigade?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And as of 1992 until 1994, September, you were the chief of security in the Guards Brigade?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: From 1996 to 2002, you were a teacher at the security intelligence training centre at Pancevo?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And from 2002 up to this very day, you have been working in the administration of the military security agency of the Ministry of Defence of Serbia now; right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I just failed to ask you when was it that you arrived at the Guards Brigade, can you remember the year?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: It was in February 1981.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And let us just quickly go through another thing, which are your accounts, your statements so far, related to events at Ovcara and in Vukovar, the topic of this case. You have given six statements to different organs on that score. The first statement you gave on the 16th of November, 1998, to the security administration; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Then, that same year in December, you gave a statement in the capacity of witness before the military court in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And to the OTP of this Tribunal, you gave statements on the 16th of November and the 26th of November?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The statement of the 26th was just a correction of the previous one, so it was just one statement in all.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. The year was 2002; and then in proceedings before the Belgrade Ovcara case as we referred to it here, first the -- the first statement you gave was before the examining magistrate in Novi Sad in the capacity of witness; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That was in November 2003.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You gave an exhaustive account in taking the stand in December 2004, the 16th of December, at the main hearing in the proceedings against Miroljub Vujevic et al. And, finally, you were summoned before that same court and the same Chamber but in a different case versus Sasa Radak, I believe?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And you were heard at the main hearing there in November 2005 in relation to that case?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I believe that these statements will also be discussed by the other participants in the case. When talking to you, I'm going to deal with the topics which are of relevance and of interest to the Defence team of Mr. Sljivancanin, of course, seeking to elicit from you your recollections of the events which are under review. Just another question regarding your biography. You went to work for the security organ immediately prior to the brigade's departure for Vukovar, and we know it was the end of September?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. It was the 28th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You were of the commander of the 2nd Battalion of the military police then?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you have any experience with work in security organs? Had you finished any training courses or schools to work in security organs prior to assuming that duty?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The Interpreter's note: Is that the interpreter cannot hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: I had completed the training course for work in the military police and not for work in security.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In this department, security organ that was in Vukovar that we are going to discuss at some length presently -- could you please approach the microphone, please pull up your chair and -- who had any training or professional or schooling experience in that security organ?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Basic training courses in that security organ that one needs to work in the organ had been completed by Major Karan, who arrived later; Captain Karanfilov; Captain First Class Petar Kovacevic; and NCOs, warrant officers Grocic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And the interpreter could not catch the other name.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said Momcilovic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Momcilovic. Yes. That is what I said, warrant officer Grocic and Momcilovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Captain Kovacevic, did he leave and go with the unit to Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: No. He remained at the barracks in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And do you remember approximately when was it that Karan joined your department? How much time had passed before that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, he came -- he arrived in Vukovar perhaps four or five days after we had, the 4th or 5th of October, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You will have to slow down, witness, please, and you will have to wait after my question, please. Do you remember Mr. Vukasinovic - and now we are immediately moving on to Negoslavci - when you got there as part of the organ of security, who did what? Who worked on what duties? We know that Mr. Sljivancanin was the head of that organ, that is not disputable. Do you know what the other colleagues did?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: The first assistant, the assistant of the chief of security for counter-intelligence affairs was Captain First Class and later Major Karan, Mladen Karan. The assistant for staff security affairs, this is the second assistant was I, myself. The desk officers were Captain First Class Petar Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But he was not in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Then Captain Borce Karanfilov, Captain First Class Srecko Borisavljevic, Warrant Officer Second Class Grocic Radivoje, who was not at Vukovar, and Zoran Momcilovic, staff sergeant, who was also desk officer and who was at Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us in a few words, what was your basic task? What were your activities whilst you were there? We shall move on to another topic a bit late, but while you were, solely, there in the security office in Negoslavci?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Could I just ask my learned friend to slow down a little, but it's extremely hard to try and take notes. It's the first time I've asked him to do it, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's difficult for me sometimes to take notes when the Prosecutor speaks in English. I'll comply with Mr. Moore's desire, however. Our priority is to keep the record accurate. Just slow down, sir. Everytime I ask you a question, please wait and answer, and try and speak up a little, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What did you do?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: I was assistant commander for staff security. What exactly does that mean? A professional helping the chief of security in organising and planning training that of the ground soldiers, as well as the military police. Control of combat readiness in military police units, jointly with the brigade command, whenever organised. Compiling lists and running checks on special equipment used by military police units and supplying their equipment. And submitting a monthly report on order and discipline in terms of the involvement of military police units: How many patrols went out, how many violations occurred, how many criminal reports were filed. Everything that had to do with order and discipline, the order and discipline regime, and everything that the military police took note of. In purely operative terms, I covered the area of the 2nd Military Police Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What does that mean "in operative terms?" Can you please explain that as briefly as possible: "I operatively observed or the 2nd military police battalion?"

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: When translated, it means counter-intelligence protection for the unit. This unit was set apart, and it was outside its original garrison in Belgrade. There had to be a security officer providing counter-intelligence protection for this unit back at base.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about your other colleagues from the -- your department, did they not have the same responsibility. This sort of operative work in terms of monitoring units, I'm just talking about Vukovar now. If know about that, please tell us, who was in charge of which unit?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: All of my colleagues, pursuant to a plan produced by the chief of security, had a certain unit, in their charge in terms of counter-intelligence protection, while the units were on their way to Vukovar and also during combat operation. Specifically, I provided operative protection for the 2nd Military Police Battalion. Captain First Class Srecko Borisavljevic was in charge of the 2nd Assault Detachment or the Vukovar barracks. Captain First Class Borce Karanfilov was in charge of the 1st Assault Detachment for a while and later was in charge of the rear command post in Berak; and to some extent, was also in charge of the counter-intelligence protection of the principal command post in Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about Karan?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: He was assistant commander for counter-intelligence, and he did not have a particular unit that he was in charge of. He drafted daily reports, which he then submitted to the chief of security.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Within your department -- or rather, let me ask you: Physically, the area covered by your department, where was that? I just want to know in relation to the command building where the command of OG South was located?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: We were in the immediate vicinity of the OG South command in a separate building but very nearby.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your department, did you hold any meetings? When? How often? And what did the meetings look like?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Just as briefings took place every evening, so did the chief of security organise meetings with us after that official meeting, in his offices. Every evening, all the desk officers would be assembled. He would then listen to their reports; after which, he would inform us about any tasks and conclusions from the meeting, then he told everyone what their job was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let's try to be specific? The briefing at the OG South command, what time of day did your meetings normally take place?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Our meetings normally took place at about 2000 hours, 8.00 p.m.; sometimes half past 7.00, between half past 7.00 and 8.00 in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vukasinovic, did you at one point receive another assignment? What was it exactly, and who gave you this other assignment?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: At that time, I did indeed receive another assignment. I was appointed town commander by the OG South commander. This was early November that year.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The command post at Negoslavci; right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: After receiving this assignment and with respect to your principal role as security officer, did you continue to entertain close ties with your original department, and did you continue to work there?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In terms of establishment, I was part of the security department and that was my principle role, in terms of my powers. But this was a temporary task, pursuant to an order that I had received from the OG commander. Other than that, I continued in terms of within my powers and authorities to work with my own chief of security.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you continue to go to these daily briefings at the security department? Were you physically still based in that still building, or were you based elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: No. I took up the post that I was had been ordered to take in a different building this time. This distance being about 200 metres from the OG South command. I was appointed town commander, so I just moved there. As for me going to those briefings, it was no longer mandatory for me to go, and I hardly ever went. Sometimes they would call and I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we now please have Exhibit 374 pulled up on our screens? Mr. Vukasinovic, you're about to see a document right there in front of you, and if you could please shed some light on that. This is an order of the OG South commander dated the 9th of November, 1991. If we could please pull it up a little. Mr. Vukasinovic, is this the document containing your new appointment?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's the very document appointing me as Negoslavci town commander; and these other persons being appointed here, Captain First Class Bozic Mile, my deputy; and Captain Sretko Jankovic, a member of the command. He was a legal officer and that was his remit and his role within that team. There was need for legal interpretation of certain problems, especially when new charges are brought against individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about your deputy, which unit did he come from, Mr. Mile Bozic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: He was a member of the 1st Military Police Battalion. And he was appointed my deputy, simply because there was nobody else to take that place. In terms of establishment, he was the assistant commander of the military police for moral guidance. However, once the commander, Major Kavalic, had left these changes occurred. I became commander of that command post, and he became my deputy.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And the introductory part of this decision - and you can see that on your screen - as of the 7th of November, 1991, and with a view to providing counter-intelligence and security protection for commands and units within the area of operations of OG South, how do you interpret your own remit, your own task as the Negoslavci town commander?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: If you look at the preamble, you can see that these measures were essential at the time. Probably the commander, himself, believed that I was the right man for that job, since I had been a military police battalion commander for a long time. And purely in terms of counter-intelligence work, I had already begun to hit my stride. We knew each other as officers, and he probably deemed me to be the most suitable person for that job, which really is the fundamental thing for a commander to do at Negoslavci; simply to secure that conditions were in place for the normal functioning of the OG South command in terms of assessment, in terms of making decisions, in terms of passing their decisions down the chain of command. In one word, to secure the command from any influence, whatsoever; terrorist or sabotage groups or perhaps Croatian armed units. The commander's remit was to make sure the command had perfect conditions for their work and were unhindered.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In purely practical terms, what did that entail? What did your task entail? What was it that you had to monitor? What was that you had to focus on? Just slow down slightly, please. We are running into a lot of trouble with the transcript already.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: In order to be able to secure all these things, I had no choice but to take certain measures and apply certain procedures. There were military police units that were at the command post. I had to use those to set-up control or surveillance of the territory where the command post was located, meaning to protect the village of Negoslavci from unchecked visitors coming in or leaving. I had to set-up physical security, meaning checkpoints, reception desks, patrols, guards, observers. And I also had to use the equipment that we had at the time in order to carry out intelligence protection along all the axes where I had no people deployed. The special equipment includes infrared fences and other such devices and equipment normally employed by military police units.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In terms of your function as town commander, and based on what you just shared with us, were you not supposed to know about anyone entering or leaving the village of Negoslavci? I say anyone and everyone, those working there and outsiders as well. Did I get that right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. This was the fundamental role; and based on this, you could establish some sort of control. Since this was a war zone, we needed to issue special passes or badges in order to establish some sort of order in terms of who was entering or leaving the command post. Not a single visit could occur to the command post without me or my deputy knowing about it or approving it. If a visit was announced to the commander in person, then first there would be a check and then, jointly with the commander, such a visit would be approved.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What exactly did you do? Did you have a situation where someone from a is a superior command - and we know that to be the command of the 1st Military District - came unannounced to your command post in your zone of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: In situations like these as I pointed out already, with visits like these, first you would check with the command, you would announce it at the command, and then if the commander is there, he approves it, if not, there must be a duty officer at the command post and this duty officer then approves this unannounced visit.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As long as it's a visit from someone from a superior command?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But any other visits within my area would be under my authority or required my approval?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: A technical question, your rank at the time was that of imagine?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mrksic was a colonel, we know that. Who was the most senior officer at that particular command post? Who was senior to whom, in cases when Mrksic was present at the command post?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: The commander is all the senior officer. There's no one as senior as he.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: For example, someone comes from a superior command, the commander of the 1st Military District, the Federal Secretary for All People's Defence, or the general staff, there's a lieutenant-colonel showing up, who is the superior officer in terms of rank?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: I'm jumping the gun a little, aren't I? It's always the commander, the commander of the relevant command post, in this case, the commander of OG South is always the senior officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Does every command post not cover a certain area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. That is fundamental. It needs to have clear boundaries, left, right, and down the depth. This person then has responsibility over a delineated, clearly delineated area. If an area is undefined, there is no responsibility. We use four reference points in the army to clearly define these responsibilities in no uncertain terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We'll leave that to experts to define that more closely. First of all, tell us a question, at Negoslavci, you were town commander at Negoslavci, right, and the headquarters of OG South was also there, that's not in dispute, is it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember which unit was providing security for the command post and the command of OG South, if you remember, sir?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, although it's been quite a while, I will tentatively tell you what forces were involved. It was the 1st Company of the military police, the 1st Armoured Company armoured vehicles, meaning military police vehicles that had about 70 or so men. Then, there were parts of the 2nd Company of the military police because a combat group was later formed from that company that operated under Susic but there were about 30 or 40 men there and there was the transport company of the military police, minus a platoon that was at the PKM in the village of Berak and there was the logistics platoon of the 1st Battalion of the military police. Those were the units that focused in Negoslavci and that I had available in terms of securing the command in Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Soldiers and officers from these units that you enumerated just now, did they take part in other assignments? I'm referring to the armoured battalion and the traffic and transportation people or were they only working at the command post?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: No. The only unit was a manoeuvreing unit for certain work that came up during combat operations; namely, to provide security for convoys in any direction, convoys of civilians or escorting a delegation. That's how the transport company was used in terms of securing the area and the axis of movement through its traffic patrols and also parts of the armoured company using the armoured vehicles, the BOVs, the combat armoured vehicles. Let me put it this way, it's a good thing they were armoured vehicles, that they had strong fire support and that they could meet the needs of securing a convoy in any direction. And also to receive delegations that came to the area of the command post to see the commander and other delegations that would come in.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We'll deal with that tomorrow. Now just another brief question and then let us try to adjourn for the day. As town commander, as you were there in Negoslavci, did you have any knowledge and did you have to have been informed that representatives of international organisations came there to Negoslavci, the European monitors, the International Red Cross, were you informed about that? Did you receive information about that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I said that in my introductory remarks. Nothing could enter the zone of the command post without being announced, let alone such visits. That is to say they were registered and approved for entry. That is what I did; I received them at the reception desk. Well, not I, personally, but my forces would receive them and bring them to the command post, further on, according to the commander's plans.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to adjourn although I haven't concluded on this topic yet, but let us now take up any of the time of the other trial. I think that this would be just about the right time to adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Precisely on time, Mr. Lukic, thank you. We must now adjourn and resume tomorrow. We resume at 9.30. Counsel should be alerted that we are actually moving court for the whole day to Courtroom 2 for tomorrow. We now adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 21st day of November, 2006, at 9.30 a.m. 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
